Treat Conclusion 1 (ImageNet tickets do not reliably transfer to large downstream object recognition tasks) as established and available as background for this reasoning; the present conclusion examines pruning performed directly on the downstream tasks rather than transferring ImageNet tickets.

Define "direct pruning on the downstream task" as applying the LTH pruning procedures (either Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) which can be multi-round or one-shot magnitude pruning which prunes the desired fraction in a single round) to the full detection/segmentation/keypoint networks while training on the downstream dataset: specifically, pruning is applied to the complete network (backbone plus task heads) during task training and then the pruned subnetwork is rewound or reset as specified by the LTH procedure; the Algorithm 1 description of IMP and the paper's explanation of one-shot vs iterative pruning formalize these definitions ($w\in\mathbb{R}^n$, $m\in\{0,1\}^n$, pruning percentage $p$ and rounds $T$). 
Algorithm 1

Describe the experimental setup used to evaluate direct-pruning performance: the authors prune the full Mask R-CNN / Keypoint-RCNN / Faster-RCNN networks trained on COCO (and Faster-RCNN on VOC for some experiments), evaluate both ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 backbones, and vary pruning strategies and hyperparameters (e.g., which modules to prune, rounds of pruning or one-shot). Metrics are the task mAPs reported by the dataset evaluation code. 
Fig. 1, Fig. 2a, Table 3

Report the empirical result that direct pruning yields task-specific winning tickets up to $80\%$ sparsity: the paper states and shows (for example in the Mask R-CNN ResNet-18 plots and in the discussion of Section 4.3) that the authors "obtain winning tickets with $80\%$ sparsity on all the three tasks" (detection, segmentation, keypoint estimation) and that at $80\%$ overall sparsity the pruned networks match the performance (mAP) of the dense networks within one standard deviation, i.e., no significant drop in the final performance. 
Fig. 1, Fig. 2a

Justify that these task-specific tickets are obtained by both iterative magnitude pruning and one-shot magnitude pruning (applied per the LTH framework): the authors apply IMP and one-shot variants in the downstream training setting, following the LTH procedure of training, pruning the bottom-magnitude parameters, and rewinding/resetting; when applied directly on the downstream task data and networks, these pruning procedures yield the reported task-specific winning tickets at high sparsity (up to $80\%$). 
[13]

Establish that task-specific tickets consistently outperform ImageNet-transferred tickets at the same overall sparsity: the paper presents direct comparisons (e.g., plotted in Fig. 1 and discussed in Section 4.3) showing that, at any given overall sparsity level, models obtained by direct pruning on the downstream task have higher final mAP than models produced by transferring ImageNet tickets (the transferred tickets were shown earlier to suffer drops on COCO); the text explicitly states "at any given sparsity, direct pruning yields much better results compared to ImageNet transferred tickets" and the plotted curves in Fig. 1 and Fig. 2a illustrate this. 
Fig. 1, Fig. 2a

Summarize performance across tasks and backbones as the authors do: using direct pruning on COCO detection, instance segmentation, and keypoint estimation with ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 backbones, the authors consistently obtain subnetworks that match the unpruned dense network performance while removing up to $80\%$ of weights, and these direct-pruned task-specific tickets outperform ImageNet-transferred tickets at corresponding sparsity levels.

Treat Conclusion 2 (direct pruning yields task-specific winning tickets up to $80\%$ sparsity) as established and available as background for this reasoning. The present conclusion compares one-shot magnitude pruning and iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) in the downstream detection setting.

Define the two pruning regimes: one-shot magnitude pruning is the procedure that removes the target fraction of lowest-magnitude weights in a single pruning round and then trains/rewinds the remaining subnetwork; iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) removes smaller fractions across multiple rounds, in each round pruning $p^{1/k}\%$ to reach total $p\%$ after $k$ rounds as specified in the LTH/Algorithm 1 description. 
Algorithm 1

Identify prior observations the authors note for classification: earlier LTH literature reported that iterative pruning improved results in small classification settings, which is the baseline claim the authors compare against. The paper cites the original LTH/related works to frame this prior expectation. 
[13]

Describe the experimental comparison performed by the authors in the detection setting: the authors vary the number of pruning rounds (one-shot vs multiple rounds of IMP) for detection networks with larger backbones and plot the resulting downstream mAP as a function of number of pruning rounds; these results are presented in the paper (plotted in Fig. 2d). 
Fig. 2d

Report the observed empirical outcome: the authors state and plot that one-shot magnitude pruning outperforms iterative pruning in their detection experiments with larger backbones — specifically, Fig. 2d shows higher final mAP for the one-shot (single-round) pruning curves compared to multi-round IMP curves for the detection setting and backbones considered. The paper contrasts this with prior classification settings where iterative pruning helped. 
Fig. 2d

Conclude that for the two-stage detection networks and larger backbones evaluated in this work, one-shot magnitude pruning yields better final task performance than multi-round iterative magnitude pruning, and that iterative pruning, which improved results in small classification settings, degrades performance on detection and larger backbones in these experiments; this statement is the authors' summary of the experiment and is supported by the plotted comparisons.

Treat Conclusion 2 (direct pruning on downstream tasks) as established background. The present reasoning analyzes the effect of late resetting (rewinding) when applying LTH to ImageNet-initialized detection backbones.

Define "resetting" or "rewinding" as the LTH procedure of, after pruning, resetting the remaining weights to either the original random initialization $w_0$ or to the weights at some later training iteration (rewind point); cite the LTH literature that introduced the idea that rewinding to a few iterations into training stabilizes LTH training for randomly-initialized classification networks. 
[15]

Describe the detection-specific experimental setup: the detection backbones used in the authors' experiments are initialized from ImageNet-pretrained weights (i.e., not random initialization); the authors vary the rewind/reset point during the downstream task training and measure the resulting final mAP, plotting the effect of resetting at various training stages in Fig. 2b. 
Fig. 2b

Report the empirical observations the authors make: resetting to early or mid training stages has little effect on final mAP for detection networks initialized from ImageNet weights, whereas resetting very late in training (the authors observe a sharp performance drop after roughly $8\text{k}$ iterations, which coincides with the learning-rate decay point in their schedules) degrades performance markedly; this is explicitly stated in Section 4.3 and shown in Fig. 2b. 
Fig. 2b

Explain the authors' causal interpretation: because detection backbones are initialized with ImageNet-pretrained weights (not random), the authors argue these weights are more stable and hence late rewinding is not necessary to obtain stable winning tickets in the detection setting; additionally, they note sensitivity to learning-rate scheduling and warmup when attempting late resetting — for example, late resetting performed right before learning-rate warmup completion causes fluctuating learning rates and degrades performance.

Conclude (as the authors do) that late resetting, which stabilizes LTH training for randomly-initialized classification networks, is unnecessary and unstable for ImageNet-initialized detection backbones: resetting to early or mid training stages has little effect, resetting very late (after the learning-rate decay point, $\sim 8\text{k}$ iterations in their schedules) sharply degrades performance, and the effectiveness of late resetting is sensitive to learning-rate scheduling and warmup in the detection setting.

Treat Conclusion 2 (direct pruning on downstream tasks) as background. The present conclusion analyzes layer-wise pruning versus global magnitude pruning behavior. Define "layer-wise pruning" as applying the same per-layer pruning rate across layers (so each layer is pruned by the same fraction), and "global magnitude pruning" as ranking all weights across the network by magnitude and pruning the globally smallest weights regardless of layer.

Describe the experiments and evidence the authors use: the authors evaluate both layer-wise and global pruning on the detection task and plot relative performance comparisons in Fig. 2e; for global pruning they also plot per-layer percentages of parameters pruned in the backbone in Fig. 2c to show how global pruning distributes sparsity across layers. 
Fig. 2e, Fig. 2c

Report the empirical observations: the paper states that layer-wise pruning performs comparably to global magnitude pruning at low overall sparsity levels, but for sparsity above approximately $60\%$ there is a noticeable performance gap in which global pruning yields superior final mAP. The authors attribute this to layer-wise pruning forcing lower layers (which have very few parameters) to have high per-layer sparsity, whereas global pruning prunes fewer parameters in these lower layers; the per-layer pruning percentages plotted in Fig. 2c show that global pruning leaves lower layers denser, supporting this interpretation. 
Fig. 2e, Fig. 2c

Explain the functional reason the authors provide: lower layers of backbones are crucial to both the Region Proposal Network (RPN) and the classification stages of two-stage detectors, so pruning too many parameters from these lower layers (as occurs under layer-wise pruning at high overall sparsity) harms detector performance; global pruning, by prioritizing pruning in layers with more redundant parameters, yields a per-layer sparsity distribution that preserves the lower-layer capacity and therefore preserves task performance at high overall sparsity.

Conclude (as the authors summarize) that layer-wise pruning is competitive at low sparsity but global pruning preserves performance at high sparsity: layer-wise equals global at low overall sparsity, but above $\sim60\%$ overall sparsity global pruning yields superior performance because it prunes fewer parameters in lower layers that are crucial for both RPN and classification stages; consequently, global pruning yields a more favorable per-layer sparsity distribution for high overall sparsity.

Treat Conclusion 2 (direct pruning) as background. Define "breaking point" as the sparsity level beyond which mAP rapidly degrades. The present conclusion compares the sparsity-robustness of two backbone sizes, ResNet-18 and ResNet-50, in Mask R-CNN detectors.

Describe the experimental evidence: the authors show comparative plots of mAP versus sparsity for ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 backbones in Mask R-CNN across tasks (Fig. 3) and summarize two empirical observations: (i) both networks have a breaking point near $\sim80\%$ sparsity after which performance declines rapidly, and (ii) ResNet-18's performance drops more sharply past that breaking point than ResNet-50's. 
Fig. 3

Report the numeric/qualitative behavior shown in the plots and text: the text in Section 4.4 states "the breaking point for both networks is $\sim80\%$ sparsity" and "performance of ResNet-18 drops more sharply than ResNet-50 afterwards," and Fig. 3 visualization shows mAP increasing or remaining stable up to $\sim80\%$ sparsity and then declining, with the ResNet-18 curves exhibiting a steeper descent beyond $80\%$. 
Fig. 3

Explain the authors' interpretation: the authors attribute the faster degradation of ResNet-18 beyond the breaking point to the smaller model having fewer redundant parameters (less over-parameterization), so aggressive pruning removes capacity necessary for the task and causes a steeper performance collapse; this intuition is stated explicitly in the paper.

Conclude (as the authors do) that for Mask R-CNN detectors with ResNet backbones, increasing sparsity leads to improved or stable mAP up to approximately $80\%$ sparsity, and beyond that breaking point both ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 suffer rapid performance degradation, with the smaller ResNet-18 showing a sharper drop than ResNet-50, consistent with fewer redundant parameters in the smaller model.

Treat Conclusion 2 (direct pruning produces winning tickets up to $80\%$) and Conclusion 6 (backbone-size behavior) as background. Define object-size categories using COCO conventions: small objects are bounding boxes with area $< 32^2$, medium objects satisfy $32^2<$ area $<96^2$, and large objects have area $>96^2$; define "rare vs frequent categories" by sorting COCO's 80 categories by occurrence frequency in training data. 
[32]

Present the experimental analyses the authors perform: (a) per-object-size mAP change vs sparsity is plotted in Figure 4 across detection, segmentation, and keypoint tasks; (b) per-category mAP change at 80% and 90% sparsity is plotted in Figure 5(a) after sorting categories by frequency; (c) per-category mAP sorted by task-specific "easy" and "hard" definitions (based on dense model performance) is shown in Figure 5(b) and Figure 5(c). 
Fig. 4, Fig. 5(a), Fig. 5(b), Fig. 5(c)

Report the object-size empirical outcome: Figure 4 demonstrates that for all tasks and object sizes, performance does not drop until about $80\%$ sparsity and then sharply declines; small objects (area $< 32^2$) are more negatively impacted when sparsity increases beyond $80\%$ — the plotted percentage drop in mAP is larger for small boxes than for medium or large boxes in the post-$80\%$ regime. 
Fig. 4

Report the per-category and frequency observations: the authors evaluate per-category mAP change at 80% and 90% sparsity and observe that rare categories (e.g., toaster, parking meter, bear — categories with few training instances) tend to suffer larger drops in mAP when pruning increases to 90% compared to common categories (person, car, chair); Figure 5(a) visualizes this frequency-sorted behavior and the text explicitly states that rare categories show sharper performance drops beyond 80% sparsity. 
Fig. 5(a)

Report the heterogeneous category effects and the surprising gains: from Figures 5(b) and 5(c) and accompanying text, the authors note that performance across categories is heterogeneous — some categories, such as "snowboard," can exhibit substantial mAP gains at $80\%$ sparsity (the paper reports up to a $\sim38\%$ increase for snowboard at 80\% sparsity), whereas others (e.g., skis, spoon, handbag) suffer large losses; furthermore, when moving from $80\%$ to $90\%$ sparsity, the paper reports that some easy categories suffer disproportionately while rare/hard categories are fragile overall. 
Fig. 5(b), Fig. 5(c)

Synthesize the above into the conclusion the authors state: small objects and rare categories suffer larger mAP drops as sparsity increases beyond $80\%$, category-level effects are heterogeneous with some categories benefiting at moderate sparsity (e.g., snowboard gains at $80\%$), and increased pruning from $80\%$ to $90\%$ tends to disproportionately harm certain categories (including some easy categories), consistent with the paper's per-category analyses.

Treat Conclusion 2 (direct pruning yields task-specific tickets) and Conclusion 1 (ImageNet tickets transfer poorly to COCO) as background. Define "task-to-task transfer" of tickets as training a ticket (mask and possibly rewound weights) on a source downstream task and then transferring the mask and/or weights to initialize and train the network on a different target downstream task, with experiments here transferring up to the box head modules where possible.

Describe the transfer experiments performed by the authors: they train Mask-RCNN and Keypoint-RCNN on COCO with $80\%$ sparsity and then transfer all values up to the box head modules between tasks (detection/segmentation $\leftrightarrow$ keypoint), fine-tune on the target task and report the network sparsity, final mAP and AP50 in Table 4; these are the task-transfer results summarized in the paper. 
Table 4

Report the asymmetric transfer results shown in Table 4: when the source is detection/segmentation and the target is keypoint estimation, the transferred ticket produces only a marginal mAP drop compared with direct training for keypoints (e.g., Keypoint target with Det/Seg source shows network sparsity $\sim76.98\%$, mAP $58.31$, AP50 $81.53$ while Keypoint trained directly at similar sparsity achieves slightly higher mAP as shown elsewhere); by contrast, tickets obtained on keypoint estimation (which is trained only on the 'person' class) transferred to full-category detection/segmentation produce much larger drops (e.g., Det target with Keypoint source yields mAP $23.94$ at 50.11% network sparsity in Table 4, which is a large drop relative to direct-det training). 
Table 4

Explain the authors' interpretation for the asymmetry: the authors suggest that keypoint-trained tickets are conditioned on the 'human' class only (keypoint estimation is trained only on humans) and therefore do not generalize well when transferred to full-category detection/segmentation tasks, whereas tickets trained on detection/segmentation (which see many classes) retain broader inductive biases that transfer more readily to keypoint estimation, producing only marginal drops.

Conclude (per the authors' statement) that task-to-task transfer of tickets is asymmetric and limited: tickets discovered by direct pruning on one downstream task transfer to other downstream tasks only partially and asymmetrically — detection/segmentation tickets transfer to keypoint estimation with marginal mAP drops, whereas keypoint-derived tickets do not transfer well to full-category detection/segmentation and produce large performance drops. 
Table 4

Treat Conclusion 2 (direct pruning) as background. Define "early-bird tickets" as the observation that pruning masks stabilize early during training such that a mask obtained at an intermediate training iteration has high overlap with the final mask obtained at the end of training and that the early mask yields near-final-task performance. Define mask Intersection over Union (IoU) between two binary masks $m_a,m_b\in\{0,1\}^n$ as $\mathrm{IoU}(m_a,m_b)=\frac{|m_a\land m_b|}{|m_a\lor m_b|}$.

Describe the experimental measurement: the authors obtain pruning masks at various intermediate points in task training, compute each mask's IoU with the final mask obtained at the end of training, and evaluate the downstream task performance when using masks extracted at those intermediate points; results are visualized in the paper (plotted in Fig. 2f) and discussed in the text. 
Fig. 2f

Report the empirical observations from the authors: the IoU between an intermediate-stage mask and the final mask becomes stable at around $\approx 0.96$ by roughly halfway through the total training iterations (the "middle stages" in the paper), and masks extracted at these early/mid stages yield task performance that is within one standard deviation of the final-ticket performance; the paper explicitly states these numerical observations. 
Fig. 2f

Explain the implication the authors draw: because masks stabilize early and early masks yield comparable final performance, one can extract early-bird tickets at intermediate training points and avoid training to full convergence for mask discovery, thereby reducing pruning/training computation cost for detection networks; the authors state this as a practical advantage of early-bird ticket extraction. 
[55]

Conclude (as the authors do) that pruning masks stabilize early during task training (IoU $\approx 0.96$ by roughly half of training) and early-extracted masks produce task performance within one standard deviation of final-ticket performance, establishing early-bird ticket extraction as a viable cost-saving approach for detection networks. 
Fig. 2f

Treat Conclusion 2 (direct pruning finds winning tickets) as background. Define "sparse subnetwork initialized from winning-ticket weights" as the subnetwork obtained by applying the final mask $m$ from LTH and initializing the retained weights to the winning-ticket initialization/rewound values rather than random or default initializations. Define "converge faster" to mean reaching comparable validation loss or task mAP in fewer training epochs/iterations than the corresponding dense network.

Describe the experimental verification the authors perform: in Appendix C and the main text the authors compare training curves (validation loss or task loss versus epochs/iterations) for the dense unpruned model and a sparse subnetwork obtained by keeping only $20\%$ of weights using the winning-ticket initialization and mask; Figures 10 and 6 in the paper/supplement visualize these training curves for object detection, instance segmentation, and keypoint estimation. 
Figure 10, Figure 6

Report the observed empirical outcome: the plotted training curves show the sparse subnetwork initialized from winning-ticket weights achieves the same final task mAP as the dense model but reaches that performance in fewer epochs/iterations (the paper states "the sparse subnetwork initialized from the winning ticket weights converge much faster"), consistent across the three tasks examined. 
Figure 10

State the authors' concluding claim: sparse subnetworks obtained by keeping the winning-ticket initialization and mask (for example, retaining $20\%$ of weights) converge in training in fewer epochs/iterations than the corresponding dense networks while achieving similar final task performance across object detection, instance segmentation, and keypoint estimation. This is the claim the authors verify in Appendix C with the plotted training curves.

Treat Conclusion 2 (direct pruning) and Conclusion 10 (faster convergence of sparse subnetworks) as background. Define the error categories used for object detection/segmentation as: 'Cls' = classification error (wrong class label), 'Loc' = localization error (correct class but poor bounding-box localization), 'Dupe' = duplicate detections, 'Bkgd' = background false positives, and 'Missed' = missed detections; for keypoints define 'Miss', 'Swap', 'Inversion', 'Jitter', and 'FP' as in the paper's Appendix B. The toolbox used for detection/segmentation error diagnosis is from the cited work. 
[3]

Describe the experimental comparison the authors perform: they analyze a dense Mask R-CNN model with ResNet-50 backbone and a sparse Mask R-CNN model with $20\%$ of the parameters obtained via LTH, both achieving the same overall mAP, and then apply the error analysis toolbox to quantify proportions of each error type for detection and segmentation; similarly, they analyze keypoint error types with the keypoint toolbox referenced. The results are summarized in Figures 7, 8, and 9 in the paper/supplement. 
Figure 7, Figure 8, Figure 9

Report the empirical findings from the error analyses: for object detection the error-type distributions of the dense and sparse models are nearly identical (Figure 7); for instance segmentation the sparse model shows slightly fewer localization errors but slightly more background errors compared to dense (Figure 8); for keypoint estimation the dense model has slightly better performance but overall error-type profiles are quite similar (Figure 9). The paper reports these subtle differences while emphasizing broad qualitative similarity in error types. 
Figure 7, Figure 8, Figure 9

Conclude (as the authors do) that pruned winning-ticket models that match dense mAP make largely the same qualitative kinds of errors as dense models across detection, segmentation, and keypoint tasks, with only subtle differences in error proportions in some cases (for example, the sparse segmentation model having slightly fewer localization errors but slightly more background errors).

Treat Conclusion 1 (ImageNet tickets transfer poorly to COCO) as background. Define "mask-transfer" as the variant where only a binary pruning mask derived from ImageNet training is transferred and applied to the default ImageNet backbone weights without transferring/retraining the pruned weight values (i.e., keep ImageNet weight values but set to zero the weights outside the mask). The paper refers to this as "Mask Transfer" and contrasts it with full "Transfer Ticket" which transfers both mask and sparse weight values.

Describe the experiments the authors perform to compare mask-transfer, full transferred tickets, and direct pruning: in Appendix A the authors run experiments using default ImageNet weights with only the mask applied (Mask Transfer) and compare downstream task mAP to the full Transfer Ticket case (transferring pruned weights) and to direct-pruning-on-task; results are summarized graphically in the supplementary Figure 1 (main paper Figure 6 / supplement Figure references) and numerically in Table 5 for ResNet-50. 
Figure 6, Table 5

Report the empirical outcome: the authors observe that Mask Transfer behaves similarly to the full Transfer Ticket (i.e., transferring only the mask without retraining produces downstream performance comparable to transferring both mask and pruned weight values), but both transfer strategies are outperformed by direct pruning of the downstream task; the paper explicitly states "behavior of 'Mask Transfer' is similar to the 'Transfer Ticket' ... Either cases are outperformed by direct pruning on the downstream tasks." 
Figure 6, Table 5

Explain the practical implication the authors draw: because Mask Transfer is computationally cheaper (backbone training on ImageNet is done once and only a mask is reused), it is a lightweight transfer strategy, but it does not avoid the need for task-specific pruning to achieve the best task performance at high sparsity; therefore, reusing only the mask does not match the performance of directly pruning the downstream task.

Conclude (as the authors state) that Mask Transfer behaves like transferring the full ImageNet ticket in downstream performance terms, but both approaches are outperformed by direct pruning on the downstream task; consequently, passing only the ImageNet mask does not eliminate the need for task-specific pruning when optimal high-sparsity downstream performance is the goal. 
Figure 6, Table 5

open_questions.content: The paper identifies several unresolved or future-work directions acknowledged by the authors: (1) quantifying actual runtime speedups and deployment gains achievable with the discovered sparse tickets on real hardware and software stacks (the work shows reductions in parameter count and disk space but notes that MAC reductions are smaller and require dedicated sparse hardware/software to realize practical inference acceleration); (2) extending the empirical analysis of ticket discovery and transfer to substantially larger pretraining datasets and model scales (e.g., JFT-300M or IG-1B) and to self-supervised pretraining regimes to determine whether transferability and sparsity thresholds differ at much larger data/model regimes; and (3) investigating hardware- and software-aware sparse convolution implementations to convert the observed parameter sparsity into real run-time speed and resource benefits for detection/segmentation/keypoint pipelines.
